subject: spaceGalley
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: spaceship galley kitchen.
Style: Alien (1979) Nostromo.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through how to design a static Nostromo-style spaceship galley kitchen prop group, aiming for that gritty 70s industrial retro-futurism look with worn beige/grey panels and warning-stripe accents, planning out the module structure before building it with the SDK.

I'll include details like CRT green-text monitors, toggle switches, grated floors, hanging fluorescent lights, the iconic round-cornered mess table with benches, stainless steel counters, and stenciled labels like "NOSTROMO 180246" and "MU-TH-UR" to sell the authenticity. For composition, I'm keeping the footprint to roughly 3m x 2.5m x 2.4m, building out a floor plate, back wall with equipment, partial side wall with counter and sink, and an overhead bulkhead beam with pipes and lighting, while treating the room itself as part of the scenery since it's the subject of the piece.

Since this is a static model I can skip joints entirely and just use the builder's part-placement system with explicit positioning. I'm working out the floor logic so the lowest points touch y=0, with a floor slab from 0 to about 0.06-0.08 thick and equipment resting on top of that baseline. Now I'm laying out room coordinates — back wall around z=-1.3, side walls near x=±1.8 — with the viewer facing toward the back wall and the front left open.

I'm settling on a layout with a full back wall, a full left wall holding a locker bank or fridge, and a right wall with a sliding bulkhead hatch door (hazard stripes, porthole window), skipping a ceiling slab in favor of exposed beams and pipes overhead. Starting with the floor as grated deck plates using a textured box with an overlay pattern.

Writing floor and wall paint code...

Better to break the floor grates into six panels using an SVG pattern for the diamond hole grid, since the browser rasterizer should handle SVG patterns fine. For the back wall, I'm planning a beige-grey paneled painted box shell sized to the room's dimensions.

Now I'm thinking through the Nostromo-style wall detailing: raised panel frames in a contrasting tone, a dado stripe band, and orange hazard strips, plus laying out the back wall's furniture run — a steel countertop over base cabinets with handles and kick plates, topped with a sink, a cooktop with torus burner rings, a coffee maker, a food heater, and a tray stack.

I'm placing more fixtures above and around the counter: upper latching cabinets, a cup rack, a recessed CRT terminal with green text and a toggle-switch label panel, an exhaust hood with a lit strip over the cooktop, and a large steel freezer cabinet with hazard labeling to the right.

Now I'm designing the central mess table setup: a long rounded-edge table with a pedestal base bolted to the floor, flanked by two long cushioned benches on either side, positioning everything relative to the counter's edge so the proportions match the Nostromo galley feel.

Let me reorient the table lengthwise along z instead, from about z=0.0 to 1.2, centered near (-0.15, 0.55), with benches flanking it on the x-axis. That leaves a 0.62 gap to the counter as a walkway, and there's still plenty of clearance to the side walls.

For set dressing on the table, I want to add trays with food pods, mugs, a salt shaker, hot sauce, and a tiny cat bowl labeled "JONESY" as a nod to Jones the cat. I'm also tempted to include the iconic drinking bird toy from the film — building it with a glass bulb, neck tube, hatted head, beak, and little legs — plus a coffee pot for extra authenticity.

Then I'm planning the walls: the right wall gets a sliding hatch door with hazard stripes, a porthole, protruding frame, and a rotating orange beacon above it; the left wall gets a "GALLEY MENU" board, fire extinguisher, first aid box, lockers, pipe runs, and a wall clock.

For the ceiling, since there's no slab, I'll add box-girder beams crossing the space with pipes, joints, and valves running along them, plus two suspended fluorescent tube fixtures glowing white-cyan, keeping overall wall height at 2.5 with beams attached at top. Now I'm starting the texture list, beginning with a grate floor pattern.

Next I'm planning more textures: a CRT screen with green terminal text and scanlines, a stenciled wall label plate, a hazard stripe pattern using a custom paint function based on diagonal coordinates, and a control panel with switches, indicator lights, and labels.

I'm also sketching out a Weyland-Yutani warning decal, a temperature gauge using the clockwork kit's gauge texture, a food tray with compartments viewed from above, a door porthole sign with directional arrows, and a utensil rack silhouette for the wall.

Rounding out the detail list with extruded utensils, a "COOLING UNIT 3 / GALLEY 02" stencil, a fridge screen reading "TEMP -18C," a cat bowl labeled "JONES," and maybe a "NO SMOKING" placard folded into the signs sheet — then I'll write a reusable `sign()` helper to generate these SVG textures while watching the atlas space budget.

Now I'm settling the materials palette, capping flat colors around 64 — off-white walls, steel greys, dark metal, beige plastic, orange/yellow/red accents, teal, rubber black, and glowing CRT green/amber/cyan tones to evoke the Nostromo aesthetic. I'm also designing a custom wall paint function that layers grime streaks and darkens toward the floor based on vertical position.

Writing box helper function...

Since static models can omit joints entirely, geometry just stays in model space under the untagged root group with no exported joints, so I can freely use b.part with center-based positioning. I'm sketching out helper functions like a center-based box creator and a cylinder helper to simplify building up the model.

Adding bolt-merging logic...

Adding rotation and flatten support to the batch helper, then I'm defining layout constants for wall thickness and positions—back wall centered at z=-1.36 with inner face at -1.30, side walls centered at x=±1.91.

I'm now working out the floor slab dimensions, wall heights, and figuring out the viewer's orientation to map which side of the model corresponds to left versus right from the viewer's perspective, so I place equipment correctly along the back wall.

Now I'm planning the counter layout in more detail: a 1.95m run with base cabinets and countertop at 0.92m height, placing a sink around x≈-0.8, a cooktop with four burners near x≈0.1 with a hood above, and a food heater or coffee machine on the right segment. Above that I'm adding upper cabinets around x -1.2 to -0.45 holding cups and plates.

For the terminal alcove I'm working out placement so the wall-mounted monitor bracket doesn't collide with the hood above the cooktop, adjusting the counter to end around x=0.85–0.95 and shifting the monitor to roughly x 0.5–1.05, with a freezer unit (0.7m wide) fitting between x=1.1 and 1.8 against the right wall at 1.85.

Left of the counter I'm placing a tall ration locker with vented slats and hazard-labeled doors around x -1.8 to -1.25, and considering upper cabinets above the sink at x -1.2 to -0.45, though I'll skip adding a window there.

For the freezer itself I'm detailing it as a 0.7m wide, 2.0m tall unit with two doors (upper freezer, lower section), heavy chrome latch handles, rounded bevel edges, and a glowing digital LCD temperature readout showing something like "-18°".

Now I'm working on the back wall: a paneled surface with seams every 0.3 units, rivets at 0.06, mapped so the panel texture aligns with the wall's front-facing normal. Above that I'm adding wall details like conduit trunking and a vertical pipe run — placing a horizontal pipe rod at y=2.28 with flange rings along its length.

For the ration locker, I'm laying out a grid of six small hatch doors with handles and generic labels, topped with a hazard stripe and ventilation grille. On the left wall interior, I'm placing a red fire extinguisher bracket and a white first aid box with a red cross at specific heights.

Now I'm adding a bulletin board with a galley schedule sign, and a round waste disposal chute hatch with a flap and handle labeled "WASTE." For the right wall, I'm planning a sliding bulkhead door with hazard-striped frame and a round porthole window with translucent glass.

I'm adding hazard stripe markings near the floor edge and a yellow line by the counter, then working out a floor grate texture as an SVG pattern with a grid of small slots over a steel panel look, scaled to the atlas resolution.

Adding solid checker plates with rivets, hazard stripe edges, and mapping this floor texture onto the plane geometry with correct orientation so the pattern faces up and aligns properly with the back wall.
